bib.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents: A New Paradigm Bridging Foundation Models and Lifelong Agentic Systems

read.skipped: Reference list (pp. 34-55) skimmed for lineage only; there are no appendices.

question: How can the techniques that let LLM-based agents improve themselves from interaction data and environment feedback be organised under one framework, and what do they imply for safety and evaluation?
contributions: We formalise the Three Laws of Self-Evolving AI Agents and map the evolution of LLM-centric learning paradigms from static pretraining to fully autonomous, lifelong self-evolving agentic systems.
We introduce a unified conceptual framework that abstracts the feedback loop underlying self-evolving agentic systems.
We conduct a systematic review of existing evolution and optimisation techniques across single-agent, multi-agent, and domain-specific settings.
We provide a comprehensive review of evaluation, safety, and ethical considerations for self-evolving agentic systems.
We identify key open challenges and outline promising research directions in agent self-evolution.

results.claim: The survey defines three hierarchical laws for safe self-evolution: Endure (safety), Excel (performance preservation), Evolve (autonomous optimisation), each subordinate to the previous.
results.setup: Conceptual principles proposed by the authors, inspired by Asimov; no experiment.
results.quote: Subject to the First and Second law, self-evolving AI agents must be able to autonomously optimise their internal components in response to changing tasks, environments, or resources.
results.note: The number 3 is the count of laws; the quote is the Third Law text, which does not print the digit. Treat as a claim, not a measurement.

results.claim: Self-evolving loop: system inputs, agent system, environment, optimiser; the optimiser searches configurations A in space S maximising an evaluation score O(A; I) until a threshold or convergence criterion is met.
results.quote: The loop terminates once a predefined performance threshold is reached or convergence criteria are satisfied.

results.claim: Safety evaluation for self-evolving agents is mostly snapshot-based; longitudinal, evolution-aware benchmarks are an open challenge.
results.setup: Review of AgentHarm, RedCode, MobileSafetyBench, MACHIAVELLI, R-Judge, AgentEval, SafeLawBench.
results.quote: Despite these advances, most current evaluations are snapshot-based, assessing agents at a single point in time.

results.claim: Safety must be assessed at every evolution step, from prompt updates to topology changes, not certified once.
results.setup: Position tied to the First Law (Endure).
results.quote: every evolution step, from prompt updates to topology changes, must be assessed for unintended or malicious behaviours

results.claim: Most optimisation pipelines prioritise task metrics over safety constraints, and evolving agents undermine legal frameworks that assume static models.
results.quote: Most optimisation pipelines prioritise task metrics over safety constraints, neglecting risks such as unintended behaviours, privacy breaches, and misaligned objectives.

results.claim: Learned reward models for intermediate steps suffer from scarcity, noise and inconsistency, producing unstable or divergent agent behaviour.
results.quote: Learned reward models for intermediate reasoning steps often suffer from dataset scarcity, noisy supervision, and feedback inconsistency, leading to unstable or divergent agent behaviours.

results.claim: Optimised prompts and topologies are brittle across LLM backbones.
results.quote: Optimised prompts or agent topologies are often brittle, showing poor generalisation across LLM backbones with differing reasoning abilities.

results.claim: Outcome-only feedback can reward unfaithful reasoning; process reward models generally give better improvement than outcome-level feedback.
results.source: Turpin et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024d; Jiao et al., 2024; Setlur et al., 2025
results.setup: Test-time feedback-based strategy discussion; no numbers given.
results.quote: Relying solely on outcome feedback often leads to the unfaithful reasoning problem (Turpin et al., 2023), where incorrect reasoning chains may still result in correct final answers.

results.claim: OPTIMA reports a 2.8x performance gain with under 10% of the token cost on tasks needing intensive information exchange.
results.setup: Multi-agent LLM systems trained with SFT, DPO and hybrid methods; baseline and tasks not given in the survey.
results.quote: It reports a 2.8× performance gain with less than 10% of the token cost on tasks demanding intensive information exchange

results.claim: Single large LLMs with well-crafted prompts can match complex multi-agent discussion frameworks on several reasoning benchmarks.
results.setup: Cited empirical studies; no numbers in the survey.
results.quote: single large LLMs with well-crafted prompts can match the performance of complex multi-agent discussion frameworks on multiple reasoning benchmarks

results.claim: Confidence-gated debate (debate only when one model is low-confidence) sharply cuts inference cost without hurting performance.
results.setup: Multi-agent debate; no numbers in the survey.
results.quote: triggering multi-agent debates only when a single model exhibits low confidence can sharply reduce inference costs without hindering performance

results.claim: Engineering cost of coordination in parallel multi-agent workflows grows much faster than throughput.
results.setup: Assertion about parallel workflows; no data.
results.quote: while computational throughput scales horizontally, the engineering costs of managing coordination and consistency grow exponentially

limits: Taxonomy survey: it reports no experiments of its own, and almost all numbers are counts or other work's results.

Authors concede the field is early: 'achieving this level of autonomy remains a long-term goal. Current systems are still far from exhibiting the full capabilities required for safe, robust and open-ended self-evolution.'
Most evaluations are snapshot-based; no longitudinal or evolution-aware safety benchmarks exist (Section 7.3).
Safety is treated at the level of principles and benchmark lists; no concrete guardrail, budget, stopping-rule or rollback mechanism is specified, and the Three Laws are not operationalised.
Cited method results are not reproduced or compared; no head-to-head table across methods.
Literature cut-off is mid-2025 (v2, 31 Aug 2025); newer agent-evolution work is absent.
practices: Treat safety as an ongoing requirement: assess every evolution step (prompt update, topology change) rather than certifying once (Section 7.3).
Prefer step-level (process) feedback over outcome-only feedback to avoid rewarding unfaithful reasoning (Section 4.1.2).
Use external verifiers (compilers, test cases, proof assistants) as feedback where ground truth exists (Section 4.1.2).
Use LLM-based evaluators for proxy metrics when labels are missing, but expect prompt sensitivity and bias (Sections 3.4, 7.2.1).
Use Agent-as-a-Judge to evaluate whole trajectories rather than final outputs only (Section 7.2.2).
Gate expensive multi-agent debate on low single-model confidence to save cost (Section 5.1).
Prune risky or redundant communication edges for security and token economy (G-Safeguard, AgentPrune; Section 5.2.2).
Constrain topology mutation to semantically valid, statically verified workflows (MermaidFlow; Section 5.2.2).
Terminate the optimisation loop on a predefined performance threshold or convergence criterion (Section 3.1).
Balance effectiveness against cost, latency and instability when optimising multi-agent systems (Section 8.1.2).
Build evolution-aware audit mechanisms, adaptive licences and provable-safety sandboxes for self-directed evolution (Section 8.1.1).

terms.definition: Autonomous systems that continuously and systematically optimise their internal components through interaction with environments, with the goal of adapting to changing tasks, contexts and resources while preserving safety and enhancing performance.

Model Offline Pretraining; Model Online Adaptation (post-deployment SFT, LoRA, RLHF); Multi-Agent Orchestration (coordination without changing parameters); Multi-Agent Self-Evolving (lifelong loop refining prompts, memory, tools and topology from feedback).
I. maintain safety and stability during any modification; II. preserve or enhance existing task performance subject to I; III. autonomously optimise internal components subject to I and II.
System Inputs, Agent System, Environment, Optimisers; the optimiser is defined by a search space S and an optimisation algorithm H, solving A* = argmax over A in S of O(A; I).
Natural language feedback that guides how a prompt should be updated, in place of numerical gradients over model parameters.
Evaluation by full agentic systems with multi-step reasoning, state management and tool use, who critique the entire trajectory of another agent.

figures.caption: Conceptual framework of the self-evolving process in agent systems. The process forms an iterative optimisation loop comprising four components: System Inputs, Agent System, Environment, and Optimiser.
figures.why: Shows the feedback loop (setup, execution, feedback, mutation, refine) and its termination in one picture.

figures.caption: Comparison of four LLM-centric learning paradigms - MOP, MOA, MAO, MASE - highlighting each paradigm's interaction and feedback mechanisms, core techniques, and illustrative diagrams.
figures.why: Compresses the static-to-self-evolving progression into a single comparison.

figures.caption: A comprehensive hierarchical categorisation of Agentic Self-Evolution methods, encompassing single-agent, multi-agent and domain-specific optimisation categories.
figures.why: Index of which method targets which component (behaviour, prompt, memory, tool, topology).
